paragraphs: Since at night the forces of judgment (din) hold sway, it was instituted to say the verse "Vehu Rachum" before the Shema and its blessings in the weekday evening prayer, and as our teacher (Rabbeinu ha-Ari), of blessed memory, wrote in the book Peri Etz Chaim, in these words: "Vehu Rachum" — because in the evening prayer there are thirteen words, corresponding to the thirteen "mechilin" of Arich Anpin, to subdue all the judgments and to sweeten through them the four "partzufim" of the kelipah that begin to awaken in the evening, namely Mashchit, Avon, Af, Chemah, etc., and also to have in mind that the Holy One, blessed be He, has mercy on the wicked in Gehinnom, when drops of fire descend into Gehinnom, called "par" and 365 kinds of judgments, which need to be sweetened, and it is good to have in mind that the initial letters of "Vehu Rachum Yechaper" equal 216 ("Rei\"v"), the numerical value of Gevurah, and the initial letters of "Rachum Yechaper Avon" equal the numerical value of "par" — so far his words; see there. Therefore the verse "Vehu Rachum" is said only on weekdays; but in the evening prayer of Shabbat it is forbidden to say this verse here, though it is said on Shabbat during the Zemirot, and only here, where it was instituted for the sake of the dominion of judgment, is it forbidden to say it on Shabbat, since on Shabbat there is no dominion of judgment, as is written in the holy Zohar, Terumah, page 135b: it is forbidden for the holy nation to open with a verse of judgment such as "Vehu Rachum," etc. — see there, and as the Gaon Chida, of blessed memory, wrote in his glosses there; see there. From this you learn that even when Yom Kippur falls on a weekday, this verse of "Vehu Rachum" should likewise not be said, as we shall write in its place.

clarification.explanation: Since the forces of judgment (din) hold sway at night, it was instituted to say the verse "Vehu Rachum" before the Shema and its blessings in the evening prayer — but only on weekdays. The Ari, of blessed memory, explains that the verse "Vehu Rachum" contains thirteen words corresponding to the Thirteen Attributes of "Arich Anpin" (supernal mercy), whose function is to subdue the forces of judgment and sweeten the four "faces" of the kelipah that begin to stir in the evening. There is also an intention here that the Holy One, blessed be He, has mercy on the wicked in Gehinnom, when drops of fire called "par" (corresponding to 365 kinds of judgments) descend there, requiring sweetening; and it is also good to have in mind that the initial letters of "Vehu Rachum Yechaper" add up to 216 ("Rei\"v"), the numerical value of "Gevurah," and the initial letters of "Rachum Yechaper Avon" add up to the value of "par." Therefore the verse "Vehu Rachum" is said only on weekdays; but in the evening prayer of Shabbat it is forbidden to say it here (although it is said on Shabbat during the Zemirot), because on Shabbat there is no dominion of judgment, and it is forbidden for the "holy nation" to open with verses of judgment on Shabbat. From this we learn that even when Yom Kippur falls on a weekday, the verse "Vehu Rachum" should not be said.
takeaways: Say the verse "Vehu Rachum" before the Shema of the evening prayer — only on weekdays, not on Shabbat.

Accompanying intentions: God's mercy on the wicked in Gehinnom (fiery drops called "par" requiring sweetening), and the gematria of the initial letters — "Vehu Rachum Yechaper" = 216, the value of Gevurah; "Rachum Yechaper Avon" = the value of "par."

paragraphs: After the verse "Vehu Rachum" one says three verses: "Hashem Tzeva'ot imanu, etc.," "Hashem Tzeva'ot, ashrei adam boteach bach," "Hashem hoshi'ah, etc.," as explained in Sha'ar HaKavanot; see there. And Maharam HaKohen, of blessed memory, wrote in the name of the Ramak, of blessed memory, that the first verse was said by Avraham our father, peace be upon him, the second verse by Yitzchak our father, peace be upon him, and the third verse by Yaakov our father, peace be upon him; therefore the initial letters of "Ya'aneinu beyom kor'einu," together with the "ayin" of "ya'aneinu," spell the letters of "Yaakov." Now, here in our city of Baghdad, may it be built and established, the custom is to say first the verse "Ki Kel rachum Hashem Elokecha lo yarpecha, etc.," written in Parashat Va'etchanan, and after it "Vehu Rachum yechaper avon," and after it the three verses mentioned; and after them one says "Vivarchu shem kevodecha, umeromam al kol berachah utehilah," and says Kaddish. We did not abolish their custom regarding the two verses of "Kel Rachum" and "Vivarchu," for we said that although they have no root according to the Kabbalah, there is no objection to saying them, since we do not find that our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, was particular about this except regarding the recitation of the Psalms (mizmorim).

clarification.explanation: After the verse "Vehu Rachum," one says three verses: "Hashem Tzeva'ot imanu...," "Hashem Tzeva'ot, ashrei adam boteach bach," and "Hashem hoshi'ah..." It is received in the name of the Kabbalists that each verse belongs to one of the Patriarchs: the first to Avraham, the second to Yitzchak, the third to Yaakov — and the initial letters at the end of the third verse ("Ya'aneinu beyom kor'einu") allude to the name "Yaakov." In Baghdad the custom developed to add, before all this, the verse "Ki Kel rachum Hashem Elokecha" (from Parashat Va'etchanan), followed by "Vehu Rachum yechaper avon," followed by the three verses mentioned, and afterward "Vivarchu shem kevodecha" and Kaddish. Although these additions ("Ki Kel Rachum" and "Vivarchu") have no explicit source in the teachings of the Kabbalah, there is no reason to refrain from saying them, since the Ari, of blessed memory, was particular about this matter only regarding the recitation of the Psalms.
takeaways: The order of verses after "Vehu Rachum": three verses belonging to Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov.
The custom of Baghdad adds two more verses before and after — and there is nothing wrong with this, even though they have no explicit source in the Kabbalah.

paragraphs: When one begins the blessing "Asher bidvaro ma'ariv aravim" he should close his eyes and clasp his hands, if he is praying by heart, and there is a reason, according to the Kabbalah, for closing the eyes during the Shema and its blessings in the evening prayer, but all this applies only on weekdays; on the evening prayer of Shabbat and Yom Tov he should not close his eyes during the Shema and its blessings.

clarification.explanation: When one begins the blessing "Asher bidvaro ma'ariv aravim," he should close his eyes and clasp his hands, if he is praying by heart. There is a reason, according to the Kabbalah, for closing the eyes during the Shema and its blessings in the evening prayer, but all this applies only on weekdays; on the evening prayer of Shabbat and Yom Tov, one should not close his eyes during the Shema and its blessings.
takeaways: On weekday evenings — close the eyes and clasp the hands during the blessing "Asher bidvaro ma'ariv aravim" (if praying by heart).
On the evening prayer of Shabbat and Yom Tov — do not close the eyes during the Shema and its blessings.

paragraphs: The wording of the first blessing is as follows: "Ma'ariv aravim bechochmah," and afterward "Poteach she'arim bitvunah," and one should leave a pause between them so that "bechochmah" will be heard as referring to "Ma'ariv aravim," and the word "bitvunah" as referring to "Poteach she'arim," and afterward one says "Meshaneh itim, etc.," "barakia kirtzono," and leaves a pause, and afterward says "Borei yomam valailah," because the word "kirtzono" refers to what precedes it and is not connected to "Borei yomam valailah," as mentioned in Sha'ar HaKavanot.

clarification.explanation: One must pay attention to the correct division of words in the first blessing of the evening prayer: one says "Ma'ariv aravim bechochmah," and afterward "Poteach she'arim bitvunah," with a slight pause between them, so that it will be heard that "bechochmah" refers to "Ma'ariv aravim" and "bitvunah" refers to "Poteach she'arim." And afterward one says "Meshaneh itim... barakia kirtzono," with a pause, and afterward "Borei yomam valailah" — because the word "kirtzono" refers to what precedes it, and is not connected to "Borei yomam valailah."
takeaways: One should pause slightly between the phrases in the first blessing of the evening prayer, so that each description attaches to the correct word ("bechochmah" to "Ma'ariv aravim," "bitvunah" to "Poteach she'arim," and "kirtzono" to what precedes "Borei yomam valailah," not to it).

paragraphs: One may not interrupt between the blessings of the evening prayer and the Amidah except to say Hashkiveinu and to answer Kaddish and the five "amens" of the Kaddish, and nothing more, and as for the practice of the chazzan announcing Rosh Chodesh between the Kaddish and the prayer, there is room for doubt; but where the custom is to announce it, one should not protest against it. Also, one should not answer "Amen" to the blessing "Shomer et amo Yisrael," for this is an "Amen" of blessings [that are joined together], and one does not answer "amen" here to blessings that are adjacent to one another.

clarification.explanation: One may not interrupt between the blessings of the evening prayer and the Amidah, except for saying "Hashkiveinu," answering Kaddish, and the five "amens" within it — and nothing more. The chazzan's announcement of Rosh Chodesh between the Kaddish and the Amidah is subject to doubt, but where the custom is to announce it, one should not protest against those who do. Likewise, one should not answer "amen" to the blessing "Shomer et amo Yisrael" — because this blessing is adjacent to the one before it, and one does not answer "amen" to a blessing that is adjacent to another.
takeaways: Do not interrupt between the blessings of the evening prayer and the Amidah — except for "Hashkiveinu," Kaddish, and the five amens within it.
Do not answer "amen" to the blessing "Shomer et amo Yisrael."

paragraphs: After the evening prayer the shaliach tzibbur says Kaddish Titkabel and Shir Lama'alot, and after it Kaddish Yehei Shelama and Barchu, and I have written above in Parashat Ki Tisa that here in our city the custom is to add the word "Rabbanan" before "Barchu et Hashem hamevorach," and afterward "Aleinu leshabe'ach" with great intention, and here in our city the custom is to say, after "Aleinu leshabe'ach," a confession (Vidui) and the psalm "Shir Hama'alot, beshuv Hashem et shivat Tzion," and after it Kaddish, but in the Holy City, may it be rebuilt and reestablished, they do not have the custom of saying the Vidui nor the aforementioned psalm, and it seems to me that I have heard a reason for the custom of the Vidui here in our city, that it is in place of the Vidui said upon retiring to bed, and I wrote to our beloved friend, the great Rabbi Maharam Mani, may his light shine, to inform me of the custom of the holy cities, may they be rebuilt and reestablished, and he wrote to me that in the holy city of Hebron, may it be rebuilt and reestablished, the custom is to say after the evening prayer a Vidui and the psalm "Shir Hama'alot, beshuv Hashem et shivat Tzion" and Kaddish, and that he heard there that this custom was established there by a rabbi who came from the city of Salonika, where there had been severe illnesses and sudden death, and a certain tzaddik dreamed that they should institute a Vidui after the evening prayer and the decree would be annulled, and so they did, and it was annulled, and from that time on the custom has been kept in Salonika, may it be preserved, and when he came to the holy city of Hebron, may it be preserved, he instituted this practice for them, and on evenings when there is no Vidui, one says only Shir Hama'alot and Kaddish, and from Rosh Chodesh Elul until Shemini Atzeret one says after Shacharit and Ma'ariv the psalm "Ori veyish'i" and afterward Kaddish — so far his words, may his light shine.

clarification.explanation: After the evening prayer, the chazzan says Kaddish "Titkabel" and "Shir Lama'alot," and after it Kaddish "Yehei Shelama" and "Barchu." In Baghdad the custom is to add the word "Rabbanan" before "Barchu et Hashem hamevorach," and afterward "Aleinu leshabe'ach" with great intention. Likewise, in Baghdad the custom is to say, after "Aleinu leshabe'ach," a confession (Vidui) and the psalm "Shir Hama'alot, beshuv Hashem et shivat Tzion," and after it Kaddish — but in Jerusalem this was not the custom. The source of the custom of the Vidui here appears to be as a substitute for the Vidui said upon retiring to bed. Inquiry made with a rabbi from Hebron revealed that there too the custom is to say this Vidui and psalm after the evening prayer — and that this custom began in Salonika, after a certain tzaddik dreamed, during a severe epidemic, that they should institute a Vidui after the evening prayer and the decree would be annulled, and so it was. From Rosh Chodesh Elul until Shemini Atzeret, one adds after Shacharit and Ma'ariv the psalm "LeDavid, Hashem ori veyish'i," followed by Kaddish.
takeaways: The order after the evening prayer: Kaddish Titkabel, Shir Lama'alot, Kaddish Yehei Shelama, Barchu, Aleinu leshabe'ach.
The custom of Baghdad and Hebron: to add a Vidui and the psalm "Shir Hama'alot beshuv Hashem" after Aleinu leshabe'ach.
From Rosh Chodesh Elul until Shemini Atzeret, one adds after Shacharit and Ma'ariv the psalm "LeDavid Hashem ori veyish'i."

paragraphs: One should not read Mikra (Scripture) on weekday nights, the reason being that Scripture belongs to the world of Asiyah and night likewise is in the aspect of Asiyah and all of it is [under the dominion of] judgments, and one should not arouse the judgments, as our teacher, of blessed memory, wrote in Sha'ar HaMitzvot, Parashat Va'etchanan; see there. However, on Shabbat night and Yom Tov night one may read Scripture without concern, and likewise on Friday night one reads twenty-six verses without concern, but the night of Rosh Chodesh has the same status in this matter as other weekday nights, and the Gaon Chida, of blessed memory, wrote in the addenda to the book Petach Einayim that an unlearned person (am ha'aretz) who can read only the Written Torah is permitted to read it at night; see there. However, it seems that if he knows how to recite the chapter "Eizehu Mekoman" or the "Petichat Eliyahu," of blessed and good memory, which appear in the prayer books in Ashurit script with vowel points, he should recite them and repeat them several times, and this is preferable to reading Scripture. And the Gaon Chida, of blessed memory, wrote that he heard from a great and Kabbalistic man that there is a distinction between reciting Tehillim (Psalms) and other Scripture; see there, and one may rely on his words regarding the reciting of Tehillim specifically after midnight. And if one reads Scripture in other languages in order to learn the meaning of the text in that language, it is obviously permitted, as the Knesset HaGedolah wrote, that regarding translation the rule that "words given in writing may not be said by heart" does not apply, and see also Rabbi Birkei Yosef, siman 49, se'if katan 1, and Chikrei Lev, Orach Chaim, siman 12.

clarification.explanation: One should not read Tanach on weekday nights, because reading belongs to the realm of Asiyah (Action), and night, too, is in the aspect of Asiyah — a domain where judgment holds sway, and one should not arouse it. But on Shabbat night and Yom Tov night it is permitted to read Scripture, and likewise on Friday night (when the custom is to read twenty-six verses). The night of Rosh Chodesh has the same status as other weekday nights, and is forbidden. One who can read only the Written Torah is permitted to read it at night. And one who knows how to recite the chapter "Eizehu Mekoman" or "Petichat Eliyahu," it is preferable that he recite and repeat these several times, rather than read ordinary Scripture. There is a distinction between reciting Psalms and other Scripture, and one may rely on this to permit reciting Psalms after midnight specifically. Reading Scripture in translation into another language, for the purpose of learning its meaning, is permitted, since with a translation into another language there is no problem of "words given in writing may not be recited by heart."
takeaways: Do not read Tanach on weekday nights (except Shabbat night, Yom Tov night, and Friday night) — because night is a time when judgment holds sway.
It is permitted to recite "Eizehu Mekoman" or "Petichat Eliyahu" at night, and Psalms after midnight; and it is permitted to read Scripture in translation for the purpose of study.

paragraphs: Sleep at night is for man a need and a benefit, even from the spiritual side, because there is a secret in it, that it is a lofty need, and therefore a person should intend that even at the time of sleep he is serving his Creator, in the aspect of "Know Him in all your ways," and therefore our Sages, of blessed memory, instituted a blessing over sleep, namely the blessing of Hamapil, but sleeping during the day is bad for the righteous and good for the wicked, except on the day of Shabbat, when sleep is good even for the righteous, as mentioned in Sha'ar HaKavanot.

clarification.explanation: Sleep at night has a need and a benefit even from the spiritual side, for it contains a lofty secret; therefore a person should intend that even while sleeping he is serving his Creator — in the aspect of "Know Him in all your ways." Therefore the Sages instituted a special blessing over sleep, the blessing of "Hamapil." But sleeping during the day is bad for the righteous and good for the wicked, except on the day of Shabbat, when sleep is good for everyone.
takeaways: Sleep at night, too, is service of God, and therefore a special blessing was instituted over it (the blessing of Hamapil).
Sleeping during the day — bad for the righteous, good for the wicked, except on Shabbat, when sleep is good for everyone.

paragraphs: It is good to take care not to sleep at night until three hours of the night have passed, and there is a secret in this matter, in order to establish the lights of the supernal "mochin" (intellects), as mentioned in Sha'ar HaKavanot, and I wrote in my small book Makbetziel that the measure of these three hours is counted from the time of the evening prayer, so that one who prayed the evening prayer while it was still day, that is, at "Plag HaMinchah" according to the opinion of Rabbi Yehudah, should count the three hours from that time.

clarification.explanation: It is good to be careful not to sleep at night until three hours have passed from the start of the night, and there is a secret in this, in order to establish the lights of the supernal intellects. These three hours are counted from the time of the evening prayer — so that one who prayed the evening prayer while it was still day, at "Plag HaMinchah" (according to the opinion of Rabbi Yehudah), counts the three hours from that earlier time.
takeaways: Try not to sleep until three hours have passed from the evening prayer (or from Plag HaMinchah, if one prayed early).

paragraphs: At the beginning of the night a person should lie specifically on his left side, and after midnight, if he wishes, he may turn onto his right side, and this practice helps to nullify the external forces (kelipot), as is written in Sha'ar HaKavanot, and he should be careful to sleep wearing his tallit katan, not removing it even when he lies down at night on his bed, and this greatly helps to nullify the external forces, as mentioned in Sha'ar HaKavanot, and he should also be careful not to have iron on him while sleeping, and be careful not to mention with his mouth the name "Samech-Mem" [Satan] even during the day, and all the more so at night, which is his time of dominion, and one should not mention with his mouth the names of demons that exist in foreign languages, since demons too belong to the portion of "Samech-Mem," and mentioning them increases their power, as mentioned in Sha'ar HaKavanot.

clarification.explanation: At the beginning of the night, one should lie specifically on the left side, and after midnight one may turn onto the right side. This practice helps to nullify the external forces (kelipot). One must be careful to sleep while wearing a tallit katan, without removing it even while lying down at night, which also greatly helps to nullify those forces. One must also be careful not to have iron on him while sleeping, and not to say with his mouth the name "Samech-Mem" (a name for Satan), even during the day, and certainly not at night when it is his time of dominion; and one should likewise not mention with his mouth the names of demons given in foreign languages, since demons too belong to the portion of "Samech-Mem," and mentioning their name increases their power.
takeaways: Lie on the left side at the start of the night, and turn to the right side after midnight.
Sleep wearing a tallit katan, without iron on the body, and avoid saying the name of Satan or the names of demons aloud.

paragraphs: One must be very careful with the Shema recited upon the bed, which is one of the four recitations of the Shema that a person is obligated to say every day, and it is the lowest of them in rank, and above it is the Shema of the evening prayer, and above that the Shema of the Korbanot, and above all of them the Shema of Yotzer, as we explained above (Parashat Vaera, section 2), and the difficulty is that at the time one recites the Shema upon the bed sleep is usually already weighing upon his eyes, and there is concern lest he swallow words and letters, and therefore great effort is required at that time to strengthen oneself and recite it properly, and the order of this Shema, together with all the verses connected to it, is explained in the words of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, in Sha'ar HaKavanot, and is printed in the prayer books and is known to all, so there is no need to copy it here, and when saying the verse "Beyadecha afkid ruchi, paditah oti Hashem Kel emet" one should intend that the initial letters of "Beyadecha afkid ruchi" spell "Be'er," and likewise intend that the initial letters of "Paditah oti Hashem" spell the name "Pa\"y," which is the initial letters of "Poteach et yadecha," whose numerical value equals the Name Havayah [spelled out] and the Name Sa'al, alluded to in the initial letters of "Atah seter li," and one should meditate on this verse and its initial letters until falling asleep, and an unlearned person who does not know how to say the verses, and likewise a woman who does not know, should say with their mouths the letters of the alphabet, Alef, Bet, Gimel, Dalet, or "Baruch Hashem le'olam amen ve'amen," several times, one after another, until they fall asleep amid words of Torah. And know that in the prayer books it is written to say "Hashkiveinu Avinu leshalom, etc.," but in Sha'ar HaKavanot "Hashkiveinu" is not mentioned; however, in the prayer book of our teacher the Rashash, of blessed memory, it is mentioned, and this is the order written in the prayer book of our teacher the Rashash, of blessed memory: the blessing of Hamapil and Hashkiveinu and the Shema, and afterward "Ya'alzu chasidim, etc.," and afterward "Hineh mitato" three times, and afterward "Yevarechecha, etc.," "Ya'er, etc.," "Yisa, etc.," and afterward "Yoshev beseter" until "Hashem machasi," and afterward Vidui, and afterward "Ana beko'ach" in full, repeating the verse corresponding to that day three times, and afterward "Atah takum terachem Tzion, etc." and afterward "Beyadecha afkid ruchi, etc." with the intention of the Name Eloha.

clarification.explanation: One must be very careful with the Shema recited upon the bed — it is one of the four recitations of the Shema that a person is obligated in every day, and it is the lowest of them in rank (above it is the Shema of the evening prayer, above that the Shema of the Korbanot, and above all of them the Shema of Yotzer, as explained above in Parashat Vaera). The problem is that at the time one recites the Shema upon the bed, sleep is generally already overtaking him, and there is concern lest he swallow words and letters — therefore one must make a great effort to strengthen himself and recite it properly. The exact order of the verses is found in the words of the Ari, of blessed memory, in Sha'ar HaKavanot, and is printed in the prayer books, so there is no need to copy it here. When saying the verse "Beyadecha afkid ruchi, paditah oti Hashem Kel emet," one should have in mind that the initial letters of "Beyadecha afkid ruchi" spell "Be'er," and the initial letters of "Paditah oti Hashem" spell "Pa\"y" — which are the initial letters of "Poteach et yadecha," whose numerical value equals the Name Havayah [spelled out] and the Name Sa'al, alluded to in "Atah seter li" — and to meditate on this verse and these initial letters until falling asleep. An unlearned person who does not know the verses, and likewise a woman who does not know them, should say the letters of the alphabet, or "Baruch Hashem le'olam" repeatedly, until they fall asleep amid words of Torah. In the prayer books it says to recite "Hashkiveinu" before this Shema, though in Sha'ar HaKavanot this is not mentioned; but in the prayer book of the Rashash it is mentioned, and according to it the order is: the blessing of Hamapil, Hashkiveinu, the Shema, "Ya'alzu chasidim," "Hineh mitato" three times, the Priestly Blessing (Yevarechecha, Ya'er, Yisa), the psalm "Yoshev beseter," Vidui, "Ana beko'ach" in full with a threefold repetition of the verse suited to that day, and afterward "Atah takum terachem Tzion" and "Beyadecha afkid ruchi."
takeaways: The Shema recited upon the bed requires special attention, because sleep begins to overtake one at the time of its recitation.

The intention of the initial letters in the verse "Beyadecha afkid ruchi, paditah oti Hashem": "Be'er" and "Pa\"y" (= "Poteach et yadecha," equal to the Name Havayah and the Name Sa'al, alluded to in "Atah seter li").
One who does not know the verses (an unlearned person or a woman) should say the alphabet or "Baruch Hashem le'olam" repeatedly.
There is a detailed order of verses surrounding this Shema according to the prayer book of the Rashash.

paragraphs: The blessing of Hamapil was instituted with [God's] Name and Kingship (Shem uMalchut), and so it should be said, according to the words of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, but there are those who have the custom not to say the blessing with Name and Kingship — and such is my custom and the custom of my father, of blessed memory — the reason being concern lest one be forced to interrupt with some words that he must speak, and I wrote to our friend, the great Rabbi Maharam Mani, may his light shine, to inform me of the custom of the pious in the holy cities, may they be rebuilt and reestablished, and he wrote to me that most do not say the blessing with Name and Kingship, and he further wrote that he saw, in a manuscript of Rabbi Avraham Alzerki, of blessed memory, that he wrote: "I have seen great men of Israel who do not say this blessing," for the reason that they might need to interrupt with speech, and there are several halachic authorities who hold that if one interrupts, the blessing becomes a blessing said in vain; see Petach HaDevir, part 2, siman 239 — so far his words, may his light shine. Therefore it seems proper to instruct that each person should follow his own custom in this matter, and there is a great warning to those who do say the blessing, that they should try very hard to restrain themselves not to interrupt with speech between the blessing and sleep, in a case where sleep does not come to them immediately, and one who is concerned and does not say the blessing with Name and Kingship should be careful to meditate on the Name and Kingship in his heart. Also know that I found written, in a manuscript of the book Keter Malchut, that one should say, before all else, before Hamapil: "Leshem yichud Kudsha Berich Hu uShechinteih, etc., we hereby accept His divinity, blessed be He, and His love and His fear, and I am in awe of Him, for He is great and rules over all, and all is as nothing before Him, and I hereby accept His kingship over every limb and every sinew, over the two hundred forty-eight limbs and three hundred sixty-five sinews of my body and my soul, my spirit and my higher soul, a complete and whole kingship, and I hereby am a servant to the Name, blessed be He, and may He in His mercy grant us the merit to serve Him with a whole heart and a willing soul, Amen, so may it be His will" — so far his wording, and so I practice.

clarification.explanation: The blessing of "Hamapil" was instituted with Name and Kingship, and so it should be said, according to the Ari, of blessed memory. But there are those who have the custom not to say it with Name and Kingship — and this is also the custom of Rabbi Yosef Chaim and the custom of his father — out of concern that he might have to interrupt with speech before falling asleep (for example, if sleep is delayed). The custom of most of the pious in the holy cities is likewise not to say it with Name and Kingship, out of the same concern about interrupting with speech, since some hold that such an interruption may turn the blessing into a blessing said in vain. Rabbi Yosef Chaim's ruling: each person should follow his own custom, but those who do say it with Name and Kingship must be very careful not to interrupt with speech between the blessing and sleep if sleep is delayed; and one who is concerned and does not say it with Name and Kingship should meditate on Name and Kingship in his heart. There is also a formula (found in the book Keter Malchut) to say before Hamapil: "Leshem yichud Kudsha Berich Hu uShechinteih," in which a person accepts God's kingship over all his limbs and sinews and declares himself a servant of God — and this is Rabbi Yosef Chaim's practice.
takeaways: The blessing of "Hamapil": some have the custom to say it with Name and Kingship, and some do not — out of concern about interrupting with speech before sleep; each person should follow his own custom.
It is good to say before the blessing of Hamapil the formula "Leshem yichud" from the book Keter Malchut.

paragraphs: In this Shema recited upon the bed one should have in mind to rectify the sin of seminal emission and seed spilled in vain that came from him, whether inadvertently or intentionally, so that the impure bodies which clothe the souls that were seized by the Sitra Achra by virtue of those drops of seed that were spilled in vain should die, and those holy souls should return to holiness and come into this world like other holy souls, and this Shema, said with this intention, is also beneficial for those drops of seed that come from him after marital relations, when he did not remain lying on his stomach until all the drops had come out, and likewise for the small drops that sometimes come from him through straining while relieving himself, and likewise for small drops that come from him through the hardening of the organ before relations, when the seed has not yet properly entered its place due to some delay he had, whether unintentional or willful, and this Shema recited upon the bed is also beneficial for a woman, regarding seed that emerges from her due to increased desire that is aroused in her, concerning which it is said, "Nor shall any plague come near your tent" — this refers to your wife, who is called a "tent"; see Sefer HaKavanot.

clarification.explanation: In this Shema recited upon the bed, one should have in mind to rectify the sin of seminal emission (keri), whether inadvertent or intentional — so that the impure bodies clothing the souls seized by the Sitra Achra through those wasted drops should die, and those holy souls return to holiness and come into this world like other holy souls. This rectification also helps for drops of seed that emerge after marital relations, when one did not remain lying on the stomach until all the drops came out, and for small drops that emerge from straining during bodily needs, and for drops that emerge from arousal before relations. This Shema also benefits a woman, regarding seed that emerges from her due to increased desire.
takeaways: The Shema recited upon the bed also rectifies the sin of seminal emission, whether inadvertent or intentional, and similar matters relating to seed improperly emitted, for both men and women.

paragraphs: If one performs a "tikkun" of remaining awake all night, such as on the night of Shavuot and Hoshana Rabbah, one should say the Shema upon the bed a little before midnight, together with all the verses of "Ya'alzu, etc.," "Hineh, etc.," "Yevarechecha, etc.," "Yoshev beseter, etc.," "Ana beko'ach, etc."

clarification.explanation: One who performs a "tikkun" of remaining awake all night, such as on the night of Shavuot or Hoshana Rabbah, should recite the Shema upon the bed a little before midnight, together with all its accompanying verses ("Ya'alzu chasidim," "Hineh," the Priestly Blessing, "Yoshev beseter," "Ana beko'ach," etc.).
takeaways: On nights of "tikkun" (Shavuot, Hoshana Rabbah) — recite the Shema upon the bed a little before midnight, not at the end of the night.

paragraphs: One does not eat, drink, or speak after the Shema recited upon the bed, and if one recited it and cannot fall asleep, we have already written above that he should exert himself to overcome this and stand firm to meditate on words of Torah so that he falls asleep amid words of Torah, and should satisfy himself with words of Torah, which "gives life to those who do it, and whoever finds it finds life."

clarification.explanation: After the Shema recited upon the bed, one should not eat, drink, or speak. One who recited it and cannot fall asleep should, as already written above, exert himself to meditate on words of Torah so that he falls asleep amid Torah study.
takeaways: After the Shema upon the bed — do not eat, drink, or speak; one who cannot fall asleep should meditate on words of Torah until he does.
